findings.proof: bin/greet.sh:9 passes the user's name to echo. On macOS /bin/sh, and dash on Debian/Ubuntu, echo expands backslash escapes. `sh bin/greet.sh 'a\tb\cZ'` printed a tab and dropped 'Z' and the trailing newline.
findings.claim: Switching from printf to `echo "${line}"` makes names that contain backslashes print wrong: `\t` and `\n` get expanded, and `\c` cuts the output short with no newline. This hits plain greetings too, not just --shout.
`tr a-z A-Z` only uppercases ASCII, so `--shout 'é'` prints `HELLO é`. shellcheck -o all reports SC2018 and SC2019 here, and the README asks for shellcheck to pass.
The header comment says "--shout first prints it in capitals". It reads as if the script prints twice, when it means --shout has to be the first argument.
findings.suggestion: Reword it, e.g. "Prints a greeting for the name given; a leading --shout prints it in capitals."

noticed.text: No test covers --shout or a name with special characters. The only test checks `hello ada`.

notes.text: Parsing the flag with `[ ... ] && { ...; }` is safe under `set -e` here: a false test on the left of && does not exit, and `${1-}` keeps `set -u` happy when no argument is given.
Every expansion is quoted, and the script uses only POSIX sh features, as its `#!/bin/sh` shebang requires.
